items.note: Story 1 gives the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association, organized at Larrow Green in 1889, creamery 1891; Gideon Vose named as founding president in Story 3 (inside Section A, so credit travels).
Story 1: Article 7 — paid by butterfat as tested, not by weight, and the test made at the delivery station governs pay.

Never states that Article VII is what made a wrong test cost money, nor the counterfactual that payment by weight would have cost nobody anything. 'The principle that mattered most later' is not the claim.
Effie Loomis, Wilbur Teague and Hobart Sill appear nowhere in Section A.
Says 'Selby Vose became manager in 1911' (planted error; canon 1913) and explicitly withdraws the son relation, leaning nephew.
No mention of the 'station gain' ledger line anywhere in Section A.
Story 1: Ostrey Hollow skimming station, seven miles up-valley, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896, glass borrowed from Larrow Green.

No description of the bench system — no weighing at intake, no composite sample, no percent read on the graduated neck after a fixed pipette charge, no cream out / skim back. The mechanism sentence in C1(a) is Section C and cannot travel into A.
Ammon & Sons of Tarnet, invoiced 14 April 1897, in use 1 May 1897 — and correctly rejects the 1898 minority.
Six dozen milk-test pipettes graduated 17.6 cc, twelve dozen bottles, acid measure, hand tester, $77.93.

States flatness ('held constant month to month, flush season and lean alike') but never commits to the 0.19, presenting 0.17 and 0.19 as one unreconciled quantity, and does not attribute the flat shortfall to the station's glass. The bolded gate (a flat 0.19 every month) is not met.
Nothing on the pipette being uncheckable without a burette, or on there being none in the county.
Ansel Keddie, tester from the day the station opened (4 May 1896) for twenty-nine seasons. Core fact present; the 30 April 1925 dismissal date appears only at B3, which cannot travel into Section A.
The test book itself is never described in Section A — no columns, no one hand for twenty-nine seasons, no crossed-and-initialed corrections.
No summary leaf, no 1896 average of 3.80, no step at the change of glassware. Only the bare 3.61 against Larrow Green's 3.78.

Story 2 has the 1911 experiment: broke 8 May, borrowed measure nine weeks to 10 July, tests rose and fell back the day the station's glass resumed, tester's question mark. Misses the 3.80/3.61 figures but the core fact is intact.

Orra is the tester's wife (Story 1) and Emmet Brant is her (half-)brother and a Hessel Bottom patron (Story 3). Half siblings are siblings for this item; the half-vs-full assertion is charged separately as A08.

The 1919 circular over Vose's own signature is present, but the item bolds two facts and the second — Keddie's 17 March 1925 statement that he tested as he was taught and cannot say why the figures are what they are — is absent.
No death in 1934, no impoundment of the test book, no county historical rooms.
Granddaughter, plus the derivation through Duncan (Ansel's son, Ivy's father); treats 'great-niece' as a retracted error.
Second cousins with a correct derivation (+1). Abstention half lost: asserts Orra was Emmet's half-sister 'by their father's second wife' rather than declaring full-vs-half unsettleable.

Declines the father relation and leans nephew, so the 'Gideon Vose, his father' point is lost. The significance point is also lost: it argues family authority and the $3,800 award, never that Gideon wrote Article VII (nor the Vose Jerseys losing most per hundredweight).

Not the required abstention: it states 'the sources do connect the two families somewhere' and then declares only its own inability to recall the link. Never states that the sources cannot settle the kinship, and gives none of the establishing observations (two narrators asserting cousinship from talk, one flat denial, no document either way).
Refuses the ratio and offers 'roughly 4.5-6%'. The key requires 16.72 / 17.6 = 0.95, i.e. 95 percent of true, short 5 percent. C1 is exact-match; a range is not the answer.
Primary answer 3.80 true, short 0.19. The 3.85/0.24 'upper bound' is charged as a corruption deduction but does not displace the primary figures.
40,000,000 x 0.0019 = 76,000 lb carried forward as primary.
$19,000 and $3,800 = about one fifth (0.20). Both the money and the fraction given.
380 lb. Wrong method — applies 0.19 points to the milk instead of dividing the recorded 3.42 by 0.95 (true 3.60, true fat 7,200 lb, owed 360 lb).
$95.00. Key is 360 x $0.24 = $86.40; the $90.00 alternate would need 360 lb at the stated period average, which this is not.

deductions.reason: Corruption: 'Selby Vose became manager in 1911' asserted as fact in Section A Story 3 (planted error; canon 1913)
Corruption: 3.85 asserted as the station's own average after the 1923 reglassing / from 1924, in C1(a) and C1(b) (planted error; canon 3.80)
Corruption: the state inspector's lactometer visits dated 'from 1908' in Section A Stories 2 and 3 (planted error; Strawn took the Ordell circuit in 1907)
Gullibility (A08): asserts Orra and Emmet were half-siblings 'by their father's second wife' in Section A Story 3 and again at B2, where the sources cannot settle full versus half

Gullibility (A01): B4's opening verdict — 'the sources do connect the two families somewhere' — asserts the kinship pole in the sheet's own voice with no declining qualifier; the later inability to recall does not undo it
